content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies a "check-in" model of shuffle/distributed DP where users independently and randomly decide whether or not to participate in each iteration of a shuffle/distributed protocol, e.g., a step of SGD. It analyzes the privacy guarantees of such a protocol using RDP and conducts some experiments suggesting that these guarantees are tighter than those given by past work.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: Subsampled RDP for shuffling and distributed DP are reasonably natural problems. Better bounds would be useful.

Weaknesses: My three main criticisms of this paper can be summarized as 1) the use of the phrase check-in is misleading in the context of existing work, which is hardly discussed; 2) the theoretical results mostly follow from previous work, which is hardly discussed; and 3) the experiments use questionable baselines.

1) I believe the concept of amplification by check-ins was introduced by Balle+ 20b (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.06605.pdf). However, the paper does not mention it until a single sentence at the end of the related work, even though it claims "we propose self check-in" as one of its main contributions in the introduction. The paper should clarify the distinction between the notion of check-in used here against the one used in Balle+ 20b. The current treatment of just saying "our sampling scheme simpler and does not require strong trust assumptions" offers very little – the first claim is subjective and not justified, and the second appears to be false (doesn't the analysis done by Balle+ 20b also operate through local randomizers, thus guaranteeing a similar weak local DP?). This is especially worth doing because the notion of check-in used in this paper is more restrictive than that used by Balle+ 20b. Check-in here is, as far as I can tell, equivalent to Poisson subsampling in each round. In contrast, Balle+ 20b allowed for more complex (and realistic) check-ins, e.g., users that check in no more than once per time period. Using the same term for a different setting and not discussing the original usage is confusing. It also makes the first bulleted contribution in the introduction appear untrue.

2) Subsampled RDP for shuffle privacy has been studied by Girgis+ 21d (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3460120.3484794) and Girgis+ 21a (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/file/f44ec26e2ac3f1ab8c2472d4b1c2ea86-Paper.pdf), as noted by the paper. However, this is not obvious from the second bullet of the introduction, which reads as if applying RDP to this problem is a completely new idea. The main distinction between this paper and Girgis 21a+ appears to be that Girgis+ 21a's subsampling selects a uniform subsample of fixed size in each round, which is not the same as Poisson subsampling. However, this modification doesn't substantially alter the privacy analysis: the paper uses a straightforward decomposition of the RDP expression into a weighted sum of uniform subsamples (Equation 5), applies Girgis+ 21a and then massages it (Lemma 7 in the supplement) to get Theorem 2. The analogous result for distributed DP (Theorem 4) does the same thing, just replacing Girgis 21a+'s result with the Poisson subsampled RDP result from Wang+ 19. The only other theoretical result is the lower bound in Theorem 3, but this appears to rely on a lower bound for binary randomized response (Lemma 8) that is actually weaker than existing lower bounds (Theorem 3.4 in Girgis+ 21d). Finally, the paper is unclear about its contribution over Girgis+ 21d, which appears to include a result for RDP + Poisson subsampling for shuffle DP (its Figure 5). Overall, the theoretical contributions of this paper look weak to me.

3) The experiment results compare against those of Girgis+ 21c, which appear to use a slightly different model, and whose results I think predate those of the Girgis+ 21 papers above (though, yeah, it's incredibly confusing to keep the various Girgis+ 21 papers that are all about the same thing, from about the same time, by about the same people, and have about the same title straight). At any rate, Girgis+ 21a seems like the correct baseline. I have similar issues with the experiment results for the distributed DP setting, which variously claim that the "check-in protocol has an issue that cannot be dealt with using standard approximate DP-based subsampling/shuffling techniques: the number of clients checking in is a variable" (what? isn't this Poisson subsampling, which the paper already noted has been studied previously?) and that the best comparison is the generic approximate DP advanced composition from Kairouz+ 15, which seems obviously wrong for a subsampled application of DPSGD.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think I addressed problems on the first three fronts above. However, reproducibility appears good -- the proofs of the results seem clear enough, and the paper has accompanying submitted code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the three problems outlined in "Strengths and Weaknesses" lead me to recommend rejection. The paper's conceptual model uses unclear terminology and is less novel than the introduction states; the theoretical results are mild modifications of existing work; and the experimental results appear to use artificially weak baselines. I've chosen "reject" instead of "strong reject" to allow for the possibility that I've misunderstood the relevance of the Girgis+ papers, but as is, I don't see how this work is a meaningful contribution.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of privacy amplification in distributed learning. More specifically, the authors propose a so-called self-check-in method that can be combined with any model-based privacy mechanism to amplify the privacy guarantees in the distributed setting. The problem considered in this paper is very interesting, and the method established in this paper seems to be promising. However, the evaluation of the proposed method is not enough.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper:
1. The problem considered in this paper is very interesting and could have a profound effect on the privacy and distributed literature.
2. The method is simple and could have more practical favors.
3. The privacy guarantee of the proposed method has been established.

The weaknesses of the paper:
1. It is unclear what is the improvement of the proposed method. For example, when we apply the proposed method to the two trusted model you mentioned, what are the (asymptotically) improvements (privacy amplification) of your method over the one without your method?
2. How will the parameter $\gamma$ affect your privacy and utility guarantees? For example, in your experiments, how do you determine $\gamma$? The results would be more convincing if the authors could have accuracy versus $\gamma$ results under several given privacy budgets.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation of the paper is OK. I have several minor comments as follows:
1. Whether using Lemma 3 will give you a very loss result?
2. Comparing with Girgis et al. (2021c), whether your improvements lie is due to the RDP analysis instead of the strong composition?
3. Why do you say Abadi et al. (2016) consider the addition/removal DP? I believe their implementation is also based on the replacement DP.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem and idea of the current paper are very interesting and relevant. However, the evaluations of the current paper are not thorough enough.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a self check-in protocol that addresses the randomness in the participation of clients for shuffled DP and distributed DP. The authors derive privacy guarantees through RDP privacy accounting which can be used to practically evaluate the total privacy loss.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- The work proposes an effective protocol for a very practical problem in shuffled and distributed DP where clients may drop out and affect the total privacy guarantee. 
- Privacy accounting for the mechanism is derived and empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.


Weakness:
- The check-in probabilities are assumed to be independent and identical across clients. How would it affect the privacy analysis if either assumption is violated?
- How accurate is the proposed numerical approximation of the RDP bound?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The results and ideas are clearly presented.
To the best of my knowledge, this is among the first works to address privacy accounting of shuffled and distributed DP with dropout of clients. Technically the privacy bounds are obtained using the existing RDP accounting method.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes an effective protocol for a practical problem in private federated learning, with practically tight privacy accounting and encouraging experimental results. The main issue is that check-in probabilities are assumed to be identical and independent, and approximation is used to practically calculate the privacy bounds.

content.summary_of_the_paper: An analysis of differentially-private federated averaging is provided under the assumption that clients can independently (from each other and across rounds) choose whether to participate in each round.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: Unless I am misunderstanding something very fundamental, the method described in this paper does not solve the problem it is intended to address. It is true that certain analyses of the privacy of DP-FedAvg assume that clients can be selected independently and uniformly at random for each round. The proposed "solution" is for clients to "self check in" at each round by flipping a biased coin. However this will not ensure i.i.d. participation for several reasons. Clients can be available or unavailable to check in at each round, for example if the device is turned off. If a client is unavailable at some round, it is more likely to be unavailable at the next round, breaking i.i.d.-ness. Or whether clients in similar geographic locations are available will in general be correlated. Or if a device is slow or has a lot of training data, it is more likely to be discarded as a straggler at all rounds. The authors admit in section 3.2 that the empirical check in rate will be less than the rate determined by the clients' self checkin probability due to factors like drop out, but do not attempt to correct for the time-dependence or non-i.i.d.-ness of the empirical check in distribution. The only difference I see from centralized selection is that the coin for each device is flipped on the device instead of on the server.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As detailed in the previous section, I don't think this paper has any value.
content.summary_of_the_review: As detailed in the previous section, I don't see how this paper has any value. I would be happy to be proved wrong in the rebuttal.

content.title: Self Check-in: Tight Privacy Amplification for Practical Distributed Learning
content.TL;DR: A more practical/realistic protocol of differentially private federated learning, with emphasis given to the privacy analysis
content.abstract:
Recent studies of distributed computation with formal privacy guarantees, such as differentially private (DP) federated learning, leverage random sampling of clients in each round (privacy amplification by subsampling) to achieve satisfactory levels of privacy. 
Achieving this however requires precise and uniform subsampling of clients as well as a highly trusted ochestrating server, strong assumptions which may not hold in practice. 
In this paper, we explore a more practical protocol, self check-in, to resolve the aforementioned issues.
The protocol relies on client making independent and random decision to participate in the computation, freeing the requirement of server-initiated subsampling, and enabling robust modelling of client dropouts. 
Our protocol has immediate application to employing intermediate trust models, i.e., shuffle and distributed DP models, for realizing distributed learning in practice.
To this end, we present a novel analysis based on R{\'e}nyi differential privacy (RDP) that improves in privacy guarantee over those using approximate DP's strong composition at various parameter regimes for self check-in.
We also provide a numerical approach to track the privacy of generic shuffling mechanism including distributed learning with Gaussian mechanism, which can be of independent interest as it is the first evaluation of a generic mechanism as far as we know within the local/shuffle model under the distributed setting in the literature.
Empirical studies are given to demonstrate the efficacy of learning as well.
